state:
Northfield Bank — Overdraft Protection
Customers may link a savings account for Overdraft Protection. When a checking transaction would overdraw the account, available funds are automatically transferred from the linked savings account to cover the shortfall, in increments of $50 (i.e., if $22 is needed, a full $50 is transferred), limited to the available savings balance. If the available savings balance is less than the amount needed to cover the shortfall, no protective transfer occurs and the standard overdraft process applies to the full shortfall instead. A $10 transfer fee applies per day on which a protective transfer occurs (not per transfer), instead of the standard $34 overdraft fee for that transaction.

Account activity, Thursday, customer Priya Adeyemi. Starting checking balance: $5.00. Linked savings balance: $60.00.

9:14 AM - Debit card purchase, $27.00, posts. This would take checking to -$22.00. Protective transfer triggered: $50.00 transferred from savings (savings has sufficient funds). New checking balance: $28.00. New savings balance: $10.00. A $10 transfer fee will apply for today.

2:47 PM - Check for $45.00 clears. This would take checking to -$17.00 (from $28.00). Protective transfer evaluated: shortfall needed is $17.00, but available savings balance is only $10.00, less than the amount needed. Per policy, no protective transfer occurs; the standard overdraft process applies instead, including the standard $34.00 overdraft fee (subject to Extended Grace through 9:00 PM the next business day). Checking balance after the check clears: -$17.00.

Customer chat, Priya Adeyemi with Northfield support, Friday morning:
Priya: Hi, I'm confused about yesterday's fees. Can you explain what got charged?
Agent: Sure! Yesterday you had two transactions overdraw your available checking balance. For the first one (the $27 debit purchase), our system automatically transferred $50 from your linked savings to cover it - that only costs a flat $10 transfer fee for the day, not the usual $34 overdraft fee. For the second transaction (the $45 check), your savings only had $10 left at that point, which wasn't enough to cover the $17 shortfall through a protective transfer, so that one was handled as a standard overdraft with the usual $34 fee.
Priya: Got it. If I deposit enough to bring checking positive before 9pm today, does that $34 fee go away?
Agent: Yes, since you're still within the Extended Grace window through 9pm today, if you bring your checking balance to zero or above before then, that $34 fee will be automatically reversed. The $10 transfer fee is separate and isn't affected by Extended Grace, since it's not the standard overdraft fee.
Priya: Perfect, I'll transfer money now.

state:
Northfield Bank: outgoing wires exceeding $10,000 are subject to a mandatory fraud-review hold of up to 4 business hours before release, regardless of what time they were submitted or the customer's tier; this hold applies in addition to (not instead of) the standard cutoff-time rule (wires submitted after 4:00 PM local time process the next business day). Wires of $10,000 or less are not subject to this mandatory hold, though they may still be selected for review at the bank's discretion in individual cases.

Case file, customer Grant Feldman (non-Premier):
Monday, 10:00 AM: Grant submits an outgoing domestic wire for $25,000 to a title company for a home purchase closing.
Monday, 10:05 AM: automated fraud-review hold applied (wire exceeds $10,000).
Monday, 1:40 PM: fraud review team clears the wire (3 hours 35 minutes after submission, within the 4-hour maximum) and releases it for processing.

Separately, that same Monday at 11:00 AM, Grant also submitted a second, unrelated outgoing domestic wire for $2,000 to a contractor; this smaller wire was not automatically held and processed within the hour.

Email from Grant to Northfield support, Monday 2:00 PM: 'Hi, just confirming - my $25,000 wire to the title company for today's closing, is that going out today? The closing is at 4:30 PM and they need to see it landed.'

Email from Northfield support to Grant, Monday 2:10 PM: 'Hi Grant, yes - that wire cleared our fraud review at 1:40 PM today and was released for same-day processing, well within today's 4:00 PM cutoff. It should reach the title company's bank today. Your smaller $2,000 contractor wire this morning wasn't subject to the same review since it was under $10,000, and already went out earlier today.'

Grant's reply, Monday 2:15 PM: 'Perfect, thank you! One more question for future reference - if I need to send another large wire like this, say around 3:30 PM, would the 4-hour review risk pushing it past the cutoff?'

Northfield support reply, Monday 2:20 PM: 'That's a fair concern - if a wire over $10,000 is submitted close to cutoff, the review could indeed push its release past 4:00 PM, in which case it would process the next business day even though it was submitted before cutoff, since the review has to complete before the wire can be released at all. For time-sensitive large wires, we generally recommend submitting by early afternoon.'

Grant's reply, Monday 2:25 PM: 'That's really helpful, appreciate you explaining the mechanics. I'll plan around early afternoon for anything over $10,000 going forward, especially around closing dates.'

state:
Northfield Bank: the early withdrawal penalty is waived in full if the withdrawal is due to the death of the CD owner (withdrawal by the estate or a joint owner), or the CD owner's certified permanent disability (with documentation). The penalty is NOT waived for financial hardship, job loss, or any other reason not listed. To process a death-related waiver, the bank requires a certified death certificate and, if the requester is not a joint owner, documentation establishing their authority to act for the estate (e.g., letters testamentary - court-issued documents naming an authorized executor/administrator for a deceased person's estate).

Case file: joint CD owners Harriet and Walter Grimm held a $15,000 CD (48-month term) together. Walter passed away on March 2. Harriet, as the surviving joint owner, visits a branch on March 20 to withdraw the full CD balance, providing a certified death certificate. She also mentions she is considering opening a new CD with part of the proceeds, but hasn't decided on a term yet.

Branch note: 'Confirmed Harriet Grimm as surviving joint owner on CD #77-4410 (verified via original account documents, no letters testamentary needed since she is a joint owner, not acting through the estate). Death certificate reviewed and accepted. Approving full withdrawal with penalty waived per death-of-owner exception.'

Separately, Walter's adult son from a previous marriage, Bryce Grimm (not a joint owner on this CD, not the account beneficiary either), calls the bank the same week asking whether he can also access funds from 'his father's account,' since he is helping settle other parts of the estate.

Branch response to Bryce: 'This particular CD is jointly owned with Harriet Grimm, who has full survivor rights to it outside of the general estate process - it isn't part of the probate estate and isn't something we can grant you access to directly, regardless of your role in settling other estate matters. Any of your father's SOLE accounts, if he had any elsewhere at Northfield, would go through the estate process instead, which would need letters testamentary.'

Bryce presses further, asking whether he could at least get a copy of the CD's transaction history 'since it was technically my dad's money too.' The branch response reiterates that account records for a jointly owned account are only disclosable to the account's own owners - in this case Harriet - and that Bryce would need to pursue any claim he believes he has through probate court, separately from Northfield, if he disputes the joint-ownership structure itself.

state:
Northfield Visa Card Agreement
A late fee applies if the minimum payment is not received by the due date: $29 if the customer's balance is under $1,000, or $40 if the balance is $1,000 or more. A payment is considered on time if received by 5:00 PM Eastern on the due date; payments received after that time on the due date itself are considered 1 day late. A 'penalty APR' (29.99%, up from the standard 18.99%) is triggered if a payment is more than 60 days late on two separate occasions within any rolling 6-month period. Once triggered, the penalty APR applies to the entire balance and remains in effect until the customer makes 6 consecutive on-time minimum payments, after which the standard APR is reinstated automatically.

Account payment history - cardholder Denise Okafor:
- January: payment received 65 days after due date. Balance at posting: $1,200. Late fee charged: $40. This is the 1st occurrence of a payment more than 60 days late in the rolling 6-month window.
- February: on time.
- March: on time.
- April: payment received 70 days after due date. Balance at posting: $800. Late fee charged: $29. This is the 2nd occurrence of a payment more than 60 days late within the rolling 6-month window (Jan-Apr) - penalty APR (29.99%) begins applying to the full balance starting this cycle.
- May through October: all 6 payments made on time (6 consecutive on-time payments).

Customer service call transcript, November 2:
Denise: Hi, I've been paying on time every month since April, I think six months now. Is my interest rate back to normal?
Agent: Let me check your account... Yes, I can confirm you made six consecutive on-time minimum payments from May through October. Per our cardholder agreement, that means your standard APR of 18.99% was automatically reinstated starting this cycle - you should see that reflected on your November statement.
Denise: Great, and just to double check, that late fee stuff from January and April, that's not going to come back and bite me now, right?
Agent: Correct, those were one-time fees for those specific late payments; they don't recur. The only thing tracked going forward is whether you have two more 60-plus-day-late payments within a new rolling 6-month window, which would trigger the penalty APR again.
Denise: Got it. Oh, one more thing - I never got anywhere with that $50 charge I disputed back in March from some merchant, does that affect any of this?
Agent: No, that's a completely separate dispute process handled by a different department - it has no bearing on your APR or late fee history.

questions.instruction: Is Denise currently paying the penalty APR as of her November statement?
questions.notes: Six consecutive on-time payments (May-October) reinstated the standard APR.

questions.notes: January and April's late payments were both within the same 6-month window.

Northfield Visa Card: when a cardholder carries multiple balance types (e.g., purchases at 18.99% APR and a cash advance at 24.99% APR) and makes a payment exceeding the minimum due, federal rules require the excess amount above the minimum to be applied first to the balance with the HIGHEST interest rate; the minimum payment itself may be allocated by the issuer's standard method.

Account snapshot, cardholder Ray Solano: purchase balance $500 at 18.99% APR; cash advance balance $300 at 24.99% APR; minimum payment due $40.

Ray logs into the app and submits a payment of $200 total, intending (per a note he leaves in the app's memo field) for 'the extra to go toward paying off my purchases faster since that's the bigger balance.'

questions.instruction: Must the excess $160 be applied to the cash advance balance first, regardless of Ray's stated intent?
questions.notes: Federal rules override his preference, sending the excess to the higher-rate cash advance balance first.

questions.instruction: Where must the $160 excess payment be applied first?

candidates.description: The purchase balance (18.99% APR)
The cash advance balance (24.99% APR)
Split evenly between both balances
Wherever the issuer chooses

questions.notes: The rule requires excess payments to go to the highest-rate balance first, regardless of cardholder preference.

questions.instruction: Which of the following are true about this payment allocation rule?

candidates.description: The excess above the minimum must go to the highest-rate balance first
The minimum payment itself may be allocated by the issuer's standard method

The customer gets to choose the allocation of the excess payment
